newsitem.title: FRANCE: Europeans to back deal on use of NATO assets.
newsitem.headline: Europeans to back deal on use of NATO assets.

text.p: European defence and foreign ministers are set to agree proposals which would allow them to move ahead with plans to use NATO's largely U.S.-owned resources for European-only security operations, diplomats say.

The ministers, who meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday under the auspices of the Western European Union (WEU), will endorse an accord to allow non-WEU member Turkey to take part in the planning stages of any such initiatives.

NATO member Turkey had threatened to block the loaning of alliance material to the WEU -- a key element of plans to give Europeans a greater role in the policing of their own continent -- unless it was allowed to take part at all subsequent levels.
"We consider the deal with Turkey as a very important step towards the creation of a European defence identity," said one alliance diplomat.

The 10-nation WEU, the European Union's designated defence arm, has Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Greece, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Spain and Portugal, as its core members, but a further 18 countries enjoy close ties.

Turkey cannot become a full WEU member until it gains European Union membership -- a policy goal Ankara has little chance of realising in the near future -- but has used the issue to underline its claim to a place in the European house.

The deal to allow the WEU to use the equipment of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) is the lynchpin of plans to allow the Europeans a greater role in post-Cold War European security affairs without a costly duplication of efforts.
France, pushed by its experiences in the Gulf War and Bosnia, has offered to reintegrate into the military wing of NATO it left in 1966 if the WEU is granted a real degree of independence.

French officials have been telling journalists that since January 1, when France's six-month WEU presidency began, agreements have been made "in principle" for the transfer of NATO assets to the WEU when needed.

But when pressed, the officials acknowledged no specifics have been laid down and there is a wall of resistance from the Pentagon which wants to keep minute-to-minute control over American equipment, its deployment and use.

But the issue still hangs on such obvious hurdles as Washington's likely reluctance to place U.S. transport aircraft or helicopter crews in combat zones, especially under foreign command, should the White House and Congress want to steer clear of fighting there.

The foreign and defence ministers, who begin the meeting with separate dinners on Tuesday evening, will review efforts to equip the WEU with a real operational capability and proposals for bringing the organisation closer to the EU.
